title: Values and zero values
summary: Declarations, the zero value, and why Go refuses to convert anything for you.

concepts.title: Declaring things
concepts.brief:
Three forms, and the rules about where each one works:

- `var x int` — works anywhere, including at package level. Gives `x` its **zero value**.
- `x := 0` — short declaration. **Functions only.** Infers the type.
- `const x = 0` — compile-time constant, and often *untyped*, which is why `const big = 1 << 40` can be used as an `int64` or a `float64` without a cast.

Go is strict about waste: an unused **local variable** or an unused **import** is a compile error, not a warning. Unused package-level variables and unused struct fields are fine.

examples.label: The forms
examples.code:
var count int          // 0
var name = "billing"   // type inferred, string
name2 := "billing"     // same, but only inside a function

const retries = 3      // untyped constant
const timeout = 5 * time.Second

var (
	host = "localhost"
	port = 8080
)
examples.note: The grouped `var (...)` block is the normal way to declare several package-level variables.

examples.label: Strictness you will meet in the first hour
examples.note: This is a build failure. It is why Go tooling auto-removes imports on save — `goimports` exists because the compiler will not let it slide.

items.prompt: You write `timeout := 30` at the top of a file, outside any function. What happens?
choices: It does not compile — `:=` only works inside a function
It compiles; `:=` and `var` are interchangeable
It compiles but the variable is unexported and unusable
It compiles with a vet warning about package-level inference
items.explain: Syntax error. At package level every declaration starts with a keyword — `var`, `const`, `func`, `type`. `:=` is function-scoped only. Use `var timeout = 30`, which infers the type the same way.

items.prompt: An unused import is a compile error. Which of these are *also* compile errors?
choices: A local variable that is declared and never used
An import that is never referenced
A package-level variable that is never used
A struct field that is never read or written
items.explain: Only locals and imports. Both are nearly always leftovers from an edit you did not finish, which is the case for making them fatal. Package-level variables and struct fields are exempt, because they are routinely part of an API that nothing in this package happens to touch. `goimports` exists because the import half of the rule is otherwise relentless.

items.prompt: `const ratio = 3` — which of these lines compiles?

code.label: both?
code.text:
const ratio = 3

var a float64 = ratio
var b int = ratio

choices: Both — an untyped constant takes the type of its context
Only `b`, because 3 is an integer literal
Only `a`, because untyped constants default to float64
Neither without an explicit conversion
items.explain: Both. An untyped constant has no type until it is used, so it adapts to whatever is needed and is checked for overflow at compile time. Write `const ratio int = 3` and `a` stops compiling — adding the type is what loses you the flexibility.

items.prompt: `timeout := 30` does not compile at package level. Rewrite the whole line so it does.
items.explain: `var`. Worth internalizing the set of things that can start a line at package level: `package`, `import`, `var`, `const`, `type`, `func`. Nothing else, which is why a stray `:=` there is a syntax error rather than a scoping mistake.

concepts.title: The zero value
concepts.brief:
Go has no uninitialized memory. Every variable you declare without a value gets its type's **zero value**, deterministically.

- Numbers → `0`
- `string` → `""` (empty, never nil — strings cannot be nil)
- `bool` → `false`
- Pointer, slice, map, channel, function, interface → `nil`
- A struct → every field set to *its* zero value, recursively

The design goal is that the zero value should be **useful**. `var buf bytes.Buffer` and `var mu sync.Mutex` are ready to use with no constructor. The glaring exception is maps: the zero value is nil, and writing to a nil map panics.

examples.label: Zero values that just work
examples.code:
var mu sync.Mutex      // ready: Lock() works
var buf bytes.Buffer   // ready: WriteString() works
var wg sync.WaitGroup  // ready: Add() works

var s []int            // nil, but append works: append(s, 1) is fine
var m map[string]int   // nil, and m["a"] = 1 PANICS
examples.note: The nil slice is the one to remember as *safe*: `append`, `len` and `range` all work on it. The nil map is only safe to read.

examples.label: A struct's zero value is recursive
examples.note: This is why a struct full of maps needs a constructor, while one full of slices and scalars usually does not.

items.prompt: Match each type to its zero value.
pairs: nil, but append and len still work
items.explain: The split that matters is nil-but-usable (slices) versus nil-and-fatal (maps, pointers). A nil slice behaves like an empty one for almost everything; a nil map only behaves like an empty one for reading.

choices: Nothing — it panics with `assignment to entry in nil map`
`map[hits:1]` — the map is created on first write
`map[]` — the increment is silently dropped
It does not compile; the map must be made first
items.explain: `panic: assignment to entry in nil map`. It compiles fine — this is a runtime failure, and a very common one in production because the nil map usually arrives as a struct field nobody initialized. The fix is `make(map[string]int)` or a literal `map[string]int{}`.

items.prompt: Same nil map, but you only read from it: `n := counts["hits"]`.
choices: `n` is 0 — reading a nil map is legal and yields the zero value
It panics the same way writes do
It returns the zero value but sets a runtime error flag
It does not compile without the comma-ok form
items.explain: Reads are fine and give you the value type's zero. `len()` returns 0, `range` iterates zero times, and `delete()` is a no-op. This asymmetry is deliberate: it makes a nil map a usable empty read-only map, so you rarely need a nil check before looking something up.

items.prompt: `var c Config`, and nothing else. Which line panics first?

code.label: Config has Tags []string and Limits map[string]int

choices: Line 2 — appending to a nil slice is fine, writing to a nil map is not
Line 1 — a nil slice must be made before you can append to it
Line 3 — len() of a nil map panics
None of them; both auto-create on first use
items.explain: Line 2, and this asymmetry is worth burning in: a zero-value slice is a working empty slice, a zero-value map is a trap. So a struct of slices and scalars is usable straight from `var`, while one holding a map needs a constructor. That is the best reason there is to write `NewConfig()` instead of letting callers reach for the zero value.

items.prompt: `var mu sync.Mutex` with no further setup. Is `mu.Lock()` safe?
choices: Yes — the zero value of a Mutex is an unlocked, ready mutex
No — a Mutex must be created with `sync.NewMutex()`
Only if the Mutex is a pointer field
Only after the first `Unlock()` initializes it
items.explain: Safe, and idiomatic. "Make the zero value useful" is an explicit Go design goal, which is why there is no `sync.NewMutex`. The thing to never do is *copy* a mutex after use — pass the struct by pointer, and let `go vet` catch it when you forget.

concepts.title: No implicit conversion
concepts.brief:
Go will not convert between numeric types for you. Not even `int` to `int64` on a machine where they are the same width.

Every conversion is explicit: `int64(n)`, `float64(count)`, `string(bytes)`. This is why Go code is full of small casts, and why mixing `int` with a library's `int64` is a compile error rather than a silent truncation at 3am.

A named type is a *different type* even when its underlying type is identical: `type UserID int` does not interoperate with `int` without a conversion.

examples.label: The error you will see constantly
examples.code: ./main.go:12:14: invalid operation: total + n (mismatched types int and int64)
examples.note: The fix is `total + int(n)` or `int64(total) + n` — and deciding which tells you where the real type should live.

examples.label: Strings, bytes and runes
examples.note: A Go string is an immutable byte slice that is conventionally UTF-8. Indexing `s[0]` gives a byte; ranging gives runes.

items.prompt: `var total int` and `var n int64`. What does `total + n` do on a 64-bit machine?
choices: Fails to compile — mismatched types, even at the same width
Compiles; both are 64-bit integers at runtime
Compiles with int promoted to int64, as in C
Compiles but `go vet` flags the implicit promotion
items.explain: `invalid operation: total + n (mismatched types int and int64)`. Width is irrelevant — `int` and `int64` are distinct types. Go removed implicit numeric conversion entirely so that a narrowing conversion is always something you wrote on purpose and can grep for.

items.prompt: `n` is an `int`. Write the expression that converts it to an `int64`.
items.explain: `int64(n)`. Conversion syntax is `T(v)` — it reads like a function call and is one. Note it is not free of consequence: converting the other way, `int32(bigInt64)`, silently truncates rather than panicking.

items.prompt: `s := "héllo"`, `n := 65`. Match each expression to what it gives you.
pairs: 6 — bytes, and é takes two of them
items.explain: `len` on a string is always bytes, which matters the moment you slice by index — `s[:3]` can cut a character in half and produce invalid UTF-8. And `string(n)` versus `strconv.Itoa(n)` is the difference between a code point and a rendered number; picking the wrong one gives you mojibake rather than an error.

items.prompt: `type UserID int`, then `var id UserID = 5`. Does `id + 1` compile? Does passing `id` to `func f(n int)`?
choices: `id + 1` yes, `f(id)` no — the untyped constant adapts, the named type does not
Both work; UserID is just an alias for int
Neither works without a conversion
`f(id)` works, `id + 1` does not
items.explain: `id + 1` compiles because `1` is an untyped constant that becomes a `UserID`. `f(id)` needs `f(int(id))` because `UserID` and `int` are different types. That distinction is the whole point — it stops you passing a UserID where an OrderID was wanted. `type UserID = int` with an equals sign *is* a true alias, and gives up the protection.

concepts.title: Shadowing with :=
concepts.brief:
`:=` declares **new** variables in the **current scope**. If a variable with that name already exists in an outer scope, you now have two — and assignments to the inner one never reach the outer one.

The usual victim is `err`. An `if` or `for` body is its own scope, so `err := ...` inside one shadows the `err` outside it.

The rule that makes this survivable: `:=` needs **at least one new variable** on the left. If all of them already exist in *this* scope, it is an error, and the existing ones are assigned rather than redeclared.

examples.label: The bug
examples.note: Change `:=` to `=` and it works. The compiler will not help: both inner variables are used, so there is no unused-variable error.

examples.label: At least one new variable
examples.code:
a, err := f()      // both new - fine
b, err := g()      // b is new, err is reused - fine
err := h()         // nothing new - compile error

// ./main.go:9:2: no new variables on left side of :=
examples.note: This is why chains of `x, err := ...` work without ceremony: `err` is assigned, not redeclared, as long as something beside it is new.

items.prompt: What does `load()` return when `useFile` is true and `readFile()` succeeds?

code.label: load()
code.text:
var cfg *Config
var err error

if useFile {
	cfg, err := readFile()
	_, _ = cfg, err
}

return cfg, err

choices: nil, nil — the inner `cfg` and `err` are different variables
The loaded config and nil — := assigns to the outer variables
It does not compile — cfg and err are redeclared
nil and a non-nil error about the shadowed declaration
items.explain: `nil, nil` — a function that silently returns nothing and reports no error. The `if` body is a new scope, so `:=` created a second pair of variables there. One character fixes it: `=` instead of `:=`. Reach for `=` whenever the variables already exist.

items.prompt: In the same scope you have already written `data, err := read()`. Now you write `err := check()`.
choices: Compile error: `no new variables on left side of :=`
It compiles and reassigns err
It compiles and shadows err within the same scope
It compiles but `go vet` warns about the redeclaration
items.explain: `no new variables on left side of :=`. Use `err = check()`. The rule only looks at the *current* scope, which is exactly why the shadowing bug survives: inside an `if` body, `err` is new as far as that scope is concerned, so nothing complains.

items.prompt: Does plain `go vet` catch the shadowed-err bug?
choices: No — shadow analysis is a separate pass that is not enabled by default
Yes, it is one of the default vet checks
Yes, but only with -race
No, and no Go tool can detect it
items.explain: No. The `shadow` analyzer lives in `golang.org/x/tools` and has to be run deliberately, because shadowing is legal and often intentional — flagging every instance would be unbearable. Most teams get this from a linter bundle instead, and it is worth turning on for `err` specifically.

items.prompt: `cfg` and `err` already exist in the enclosing function. What should the line inside the `if` block use instead of `:=`?
items.explain: `=`. Plain assignment reaches the variables that already exist rather than creating new ones in the inner scope. A reliable habit: use `:=` when you are introducing a name, `=` when you are updating one.
